title: The Truman Doctrine Speech
speaker: Harry S. Truman
before: By late 1946 Britain had told the United States that its declining economy left it unable to go on supporting the Greek government against the guerrillas of the Communist Party of Greece, and Turkey was under Soviet pressure over the Turkish Straits. On 12 March 1947 President Harry S. Truman asked a joint session of Congress, where the Republicans held both houses, for aid to both countries.
excerpt: I believe that it must be the policy of the United States to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures.
source: Address before a joint session of Congress, 12 March 1947; a work of the United States government.
after: In May 1947 Congress approved $400 million in military and economic aid to Greece and Turkey, and the aid helped the Greek government defeat the Communist guerrillas. The doctrine became a basis of American containment policy in the Cold War, followed by the Marshall Plan and NATO in 1949. Walter Lippmann questioned its open-ended pledge, and others argued that the Greek monarchy it defended was itself repressive.

title: Marshall's Speech at Harvard
speaker: George C. Marshall
before: Two years after the end of the war, Europe's economy was still badly dislocated, and six weeks of talks with the Soviets in Moscow on rebuilding Germany had failed. Secretary of State George C. Marshall used his address at Harvard University to offer American aid for European recovery. Charles Bohlen wrote it at his request; it gave virtually no details or numbers and asked the Europeans to draw up their own plan.
excerpt: Our policy is directed not against any country or doctrine but against hunger, poverty, desperation, and chaos.
source: Secretary of State George C. Marshall's remarks at Harvard University, 5 June 1947, as delivered; a work of the United States government.
after: Ernest Bevin and Georges Bidault at once prepared a European response, which led to the Committee of European Economic Co-operation. Stalin ordered the Eastern Bloc to stay out, and Andrei Vyshinsky told the United Nations the plan used aid as an instrument of political pressure. From April 1948 the United States transferred $13.3 billion to European economies over four years.
notes: Marshall has no encyclopedia entry yet, so speakerSlug is empty. The Wikisource text is the speech as delivered (with its unscripted opening and closing remarks); the Marshall Plan article quotes another version of the text ('Our policy is not directed against any country, but against hunger, poverty, desperation and chaos'), so the excerpt follows the imported text, not the article.

title: Eisenhower's Atoms for Peace Address
speaker: Dwight D. Eisenhower
place: United Nations General Assembly, New York City
before: Atomic development was then held under strict secrecy, and the Soviet Union, as the President told the Assembly, also knew the secret of the bomb. Dwight D. Eisenhower, invited by Secretary General Hammarskjöld after the Bermuda Conference with Britain and France, addressed the UN General Assembly. The speech was part of a media campaign, Operation Candor, to tell the American public of the risks and hopes of a nuclear future.
excerpt: It is not enough to take this weapon out of the hands of the soldiers. It must be put into the hands of those who will know how to strip its military casing and adapt it to the arts of peace.
source: Address to the United Nations General Assembly, 8 December 1953; a work of the United States government.
after: An Atoms for Peace programme supplied equipment and information to schools, hospitals and research institutions in the United States and abroad; the first reactors of Israel and Pakistan were built under it. It laid the ground for the International Atomic Energy Agency and the Non-Proliferation Treaty, but also gave political cover for an American build-up from 1,005 to 20,000 nuclear weapons under Eisenhower.
notes: No entry yet for what followed (Atoms for Peace, the IAEA, the Non-Proliferation Treaty), so led is empty. The Wikisource transcription has slips the editor may want in $FIXES (fetch-speech-texts.ps1), to be checked against the Eisenhower Library's copy: 'I, who has spent' (the Wikipedia article quotes 'who have spent'), 'idle works' (words?), 'These is at least one new avenue' (There is), 'we much start' (must), 'over shadows', 'the United Stats', 'every where' and 'lead this work out of fear' (world?). The excerpt avoids all of them.

title: Kennedy at Rice: We Choose to Go to the Moon
speaker: John F. Kennedy
before: The flight of Yuri Gagarin in April 1961 had deepened the American sense of losing the Space Race to the Soviet Union, and in May 1961 John F. Kennedy asked Congress to land a man on the Moon before the decade was out; a Gallup poll found 58 percent of Americans opposed. Visiting NASA's new Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston, he spoke to about 40,000 people at Rice Stadium, in a speech drafted by Ted Sorensen.
excerpt: But why, some say, the moon? Why choose this as our goal? And they may well ask why climb the highest mountain? Why, 35 years ago, fly the Atlantic? Why does Rice play Texas? We choose to go to the moon.
source: Address at Rice University on the Nation's Space Effort, 12 September 1962, as delivered, with the interruptions for applause marked; a work of the United States government.
after: Disquiet about the cost went on: Eisenhower called spending $40 billion to reach the Moon “just nuts”, and a budget cut was only narrowly averted. Kennedy proposed a joint expedition to the Moon again at the UN in September 1963, but Khrushchev stayed cautious, and the idea was dropped after Kennedy's assassination that November. Apollo 11 landed on the Moon in July 1969.
notes: The Wikisource text is as delivered and keeps the marks '(interrupted by applause)' inside three paragraphs; the editor may want them dropped by a $FIXES entry. There is no encyclopedia entry for Apollo 11 or the Apollo programme, so led has only the Space Race.

title: Johnson's Voting Rights Address: We Shall Overcome
speaker: Lyndon B. Johnson
before: On 7 March 1965 state troopers and county possemen charged about 600 unarmed marchers for voting rights on the Edmund Pettus Bridge at Selma, Alabama, a day that became known as Bloody Sunday, and after a second march the minister James Reeb was beaten to death. On 15 March President Lyndon B. Johnson addressed a televised joint session of Congress and asked it to pass a voting rights bill.
excerpt: Their cause must be our cause too. Because it is not just Negroes, but really it is all of us, who must overcome the crippling legacy of bigotry and injustice. And we shall overcome.
source: Special Message to the Congress: The American Promise, 15 March 1965, as delivered and printed in the Public Papers of the Presidents; a work of the United States government.
after: Martin Luther King Jr. wired Johnson that it was “the most moving eloquent unequivocal and passionate plea for human rights ever made by any president of this nation”; James Forman quipped that Johnson had “spoiled a good song”. The bill was introduced two days later and signed on 6 August 1965 as the Voting Rights Act, with King, Rosa Parks and John Lewis present.
notes: Imported in nine source rows so that the eight subheadings the Public Papers print (THE RIGHT TO VOTE, WE SHALL OVERCOME and the rest), which were not spoken, are left out. The checker flags the word Presidents in the source line: the citation (Public Papers of the Presidents of the United States: Lyndon B. Johnson, 1965, vol. I, entry 107) is from the Wikisource page header, not the article. The excerpt keeps the period's word 'Negroes' as the source prints it.
